chuukeseSentenceGuide.overview: A comprehensive instructional guide explaining how Chuukese grammar, sentence structure, pronouns, possession, directionals, reduplication, and morphology work, based fully on dictionary imports and traditional linguistic rules.

vowelSystem.description: The Chuukese vowel system uses modern diacritics. Older spellings may differ, especially with ö → é transformations.
lookupNotes: Words formerly spelled with 'ö' must now be looked up under 'é'.
Some Chuuk Lagoon dialects pronounce 'l' like 'n', so words may appear under either letter.
Some words begin with double-consonants or double-vowels.

sentenceStructure.notes: Chuukese strongly prefers verb-first order, affecting emphasis and flow.

notes: Some verbs drop the final vowel when adding a suffix. (Marked as *)
Many dictionary entries list suffix patterns unique to each verb.

directionals.notes: Directionals modify meaning significantly and are attached after pronoun suffixes.

notes: Stand-alone pronouns also carry tense when used with auxiliaries.
Dictionary shows past/present/future forms for each pronoun.

examples.english: my God (inanimate ending used as exception)

standAlonePossessives.rule: A stand-alone possessive is used when no suffix possession is present.

possession.suffixPossession: Nouns that end in possessive forms (-i, -um, -an, etc.) require suffixes rather than stand-alone possessives.

nominalizers.description: Convert verbs into nouns describing actions, states, or results.

countingClassifiers.notes: Used with numbers to classify counted items appropriately.

keyRules: Pronoun suffixes attach directly to verbs.
Directional suffixes modify the verb’s movement and direction.
A noun uses either a stand-alone possessive OR a suffix, not both.
Many verbs drop the final vowel before adding suffixes.
Reduplication changes the meaning (intensity, repetition, plural action).
Inclusive (kich) and exclusive (kem) distinctions are essential.
Some words begin with double consonants, which affects dictionary order.
Legacy vowel 'ö' is now written as 'é'.
L is pronounced like N in some dialects, affecting word location.
